item.title: We Never Called It Frisco
item.content:encoded:
They say we’re a town full of losers. They say we’re eccentric, eclectic—marginal. Maybe I’m exaggerating. But when somebody on the East Coast starts talking about a rivalry between New York and San Francisco the truth is they’re trying to

They say we’re a town full of losers. They say we’re eccentric, eclectic—marginal. Maybe I’m exaggerating. But when somebody on the East Coast starts talking about a rivalry between New York and San Francisco the truth is they’re trying to shaft us. They’re saying they’re the best. They’re snobs. But I suppose we’re snobs, too. Here in San Francisco we’re proud to be the opposition. We’re glad to be living on what New Yorkers regard as the wrong coast, with the wrong publishers, galleries, reputations. We are what we are. And damn the rest of them. Call me old-fashioned, but I’m still flying the flag for the San Francisco Renaissance, all the poetry readings, mimeographed magazines, improvised galleries, experimental films.

Of course, I’m just kidding around here. Sort of kidding around. We weren’t—we aren’t—against East Coast success. Not really. Consider Mike, with his East Coast awards, still one of us. He’s the real deal, though some of his poems, beautiful as they are, are a little too muffled for my taste. I’ve said that to him—and he’s okay with it. He knows I think Partly Cloudy and Cooler is a great book. Mike is Indian, Indian from the subcontinent. He’s half Indian, to be precise. Father was some kind of import-export guy from Bombay. Met his mother in San Francisco. They went back to India. Then she bailed. Years ago, she appeared at a couple of Mike’s readings, around the time his poems were starting to pick up a following. She was much taller than Mike, noisily talking to all Mike’s friends, nothing like Mike. Mike, with his sharp features and small, dark hands, is probably at the Silver Spur right now, nursing his glass of vodka, two rocks, no twist. (Years ago I did some bartending.) He has a great head of hair, I’ll give him that, thick Indian hair. Still living on the floor of a Victorian in the Haight that he bought a dozen years ago when they were dirt cheap, the down payment from his first Guggenheim. He’s very proud of a group of small Rajput paintings, bought from Ray Lewis years ago, when Ray was just starting out, supplying Piranesi etchings of the sights of Rome to Nob Hill decorators but really into Indian miniatures, Islamic calligraphy, and other stuff he just thought was cool. “My Indian heritage,” Mike says, only half ironically, about those miniatures with the tiny figures bowing to each other.

Mike reappeared last week. There he was in the late afternoon, sitting at the far end of the bar at the Silver Spur. (I prefer a booth.) I happened to be in SF for a couple of days, printing a broadside for a poetry event in Bolinas. I was happy with the way it was going. I’d started to put it together, using a funky old set of Garamond type, all caps, but a couple of the vowels, the A and the E, were so worn they weren’t printing. I substituted a stark sans serif for those letters, and the result was kind of wonderful, the As and Es making a jazzy pattern weaving in and out around the Old World Garamond. Although I’m content and maybe more than content spending most of my time here in Marin, things do get slow. As long as I can avoid rush hour traffic on the Golden Gate Bridge, I enjoy coming into the city to work on an interesting job, maybe hook up with some of the gang, sleep on the daybed in my shop—if it’s just for a few days. Anyway, I was taking a break from the Bolinas broadside. I went over to the Silver Spur. Sat with Mike. He’d just spent a week in New York on some sort of awards panel. He made some cryptic remarks about how badly best-selling novelists behave when it comes to distributing money among up-and-coming authors. I’m not sure exactly what he said. He speaks softly, not looking at you when he talks, facing forward on his barstool, elbows resting on the bar, so he’s a little hard to hear, even in the late afternoon, before any money’s been dropped in the jukebox.

But this isn’t about Mike; this is about Marcia, who also had some success back east. Of course Mike and Marcia knew each other. They both went back to Berkeley days. So do I. Marcia, with her dark bangs, was voluptuous or fat, depending on how you saw it. Zaftig is probably the word. If I hesitate it’s only because the Yiddish sounds a little odd, coming out of my formerly Protestant mouth. I was born a few hours south of here, in Carmel. My dad was an architect who’d trained in London; he’d grown up there but had the wanderlust, so he would say, and found his way to California. Anyway, Marcia was the leader of our college crew. She was bossy, sometimes overbearing, but I wonder if we would’ve ever had a party if Marcia hadn’t said, “Let’s have a party!” Mike, although he hung around with us, seemed a little too straight arrow. Always the diplomat. Marcia called him “the ambassador,” behind his back. She was catty like a schoolgirl, mean about the people she’d tossed out of the club or at least threatened to dump. Marcia and Mike bonded later, a few years after Berkeley, bored or maybe annoyed by what they regarded as the daydreamers among us. I guess I’m one of the dreamers.

Frankly I’m not always all that clear about the difference between what we were like in college and what we were like a little later—or now, twenty-some-odd years later. Did we think of Marcia as girlish back then, when she actually was a girl? And what of Jack (John to you) Johanson? I wonder if I’m confusing the Jack I knew back then with Jack a few years later. When we were still kids the moustache and the cowboy swagger looked a little camp. Marcia kidded that he’d woken up one morning and decided he was in some old Hollywood Western. I remember her saying that to his face. Now that he’s had some paintings hanging at the Museum of Modern Art, I guess people think the moustache—it’s developed the slightest touch of gray—looks old masterish. Marcia wouldn’t give him an inch. “Those paintings only hung at the Modern for a couple of months, the museum didn’t buy anything, so what’s the big deal?” Marcia liked to say it was Evelyn, Jack’s wife, who was the really talented painter. “Evelyn knew how to let loose,” I heard Marcia announce on more than one occasion. Of course Evelyn had stopped painting practically as soon as she met Jack. I wonder how many of her things Marcia ever actually saw. But Marcia had a point to make, not so much to put Evelyn up as to put Jack down.

As for me, I’m not good for much of anything except keeping the old printing press running. I still know how to improvise a new part when an old one breaks down. I’ve managed to keep my little enterprise more or less moving forward, getting out the magazine, Velocipede I call it, a couple of times a year, publishing a few books of somebody else’s poems, and then, once or twice, my own. I was just getting the press rolling when Marcia and I were together, a decade out of Berkeley. Since then I’ve made a living from it—barely. Marcia proofread the very first issue of Velocipede. She was terrific, a whiz when it came to straightening out grammatical messes. If we’d stuck together it might not have taken me another eighteen months to publish the second issue. But whatever it was that Marcia and I were up to back then, Marcia was too restless (or relentless) to really settle in with a guy she’d first slept with way back in senior year. I was okay with its being over, although it was a hassle finding a new place to live. I liked her, but she also got on my nerves. Then, flash forward, Marcia was back on our coast after her triumphant five or six years in New York, and suddenly Marcia and I had been shacked up for two years. Or I’d been shacked up with her, it was her house, after all. Her time in New York had come to an end, for reasons I never entirely understood. She could have stayed in Manhattan despite some career disappointments. If she had, I’m convinced she would’ve done damn well. Instead she chose to come back here and hang out with her old friends—despite all the bellyaching she’d done about San Francisco before she left and continued to do even after her return.

But I guess I should begin at the end, or at least the beginning of the end. Which means San Francisco’s War Memorial Opera House, officialdom incarnate, the full treatment: marble, red carpets, polished brass, everything academically symmetrical, twinkle twinkle of bright light refracted o cut crystal. “Oh shit,” had been my reaction when Marcia announced that we were going to see yet another farewell tour by Martha Graham, the old bag still dragging around the stage. The piece was called Cortege of Eagles. I think she quit dancing later that year. Easy for Marcia to say we should go see Martha Graham. She never learned to drive and expected me to find parking right in front of the Opera House: “You know how I hate to walk,” she liked to remind me.

“We’ve got comps,” was her reply to my, “Who wants to see Graham, anyway?” “It’ll be a goof,” she added, “a goof, Burt.” Marcia still got comps, lots of them. Even though she was no longer writing about books, plays, and art exhibitions, there were people who couldn’t quite believe it. So the publicists for writers, theaters, and museums kept writing and phoning, even offering to fly her back to New York to see this or that, once or twice mentioning a free trip to Europe. She’d get off the phone and growl at me. Whatever the project, her reaction was the same. “I’m sure it’ll be a fiasco. I’m going to hate it. And I don’t have the patience for any more hate. Which means I have nothing more to say. I’ve written the curmudgeon out of myself.” There was a lift in her voice as she explained herself to me. “I’m a changed woman,” she announced, only half sarcastically. She certainly didn’t mind that there were people who figured her career was going to flame up again, with the latest Broadway sensation receiving the full Marcia Lang treatment in The New Yorker or who knows where else.

So there I was, coming down the aisle at the Opera House after a quick pre-performance leak, slipping past rows of what back in college we’d called the squares, Pacific Heights professionals left and right, some of them still milling around in the aisles, making it harder to get by. Marcia was way up front, nothing but the best for Marcia. She was standing in the aisle, bent over Virginia Adams. Ginny, her long hair just beginning to turn gray—I think she was a few years older than us, maybe close to fifty—was in a Mexican muumuu, huge African beads hanging off her skinny neck. She was giving Marcia a fixed, concentrated look. Ginny just barely survives on some sad do-gooder part-time job. But the Opera House manager or assistant manager was one of our old Berkeley buddies. Back in 1949 or 1950 he’d directed a Pirandello that he claimed was a West Coast premiere. He gives Ginny a ticket when he can. “Poor Ginny,” Marcia whispered to me as the lights were going down, “she has aches and pains in every bone of that undernourished body of hers. She makes me glad I’m overweight. Wow. The old gang’s sure all here. They must have been having trouble selling seats, if Ginny got a freebie. Funny. We thought Martha was so important when we were in college, and now everybody’s here to watch her fall at on her face-lifted face. I really could write this up. Do a job on it.”

Heavy curtain up; the moaning of sentimental strings; lights rising on some wedges and rectangles of scenery, guys and girls, the guys practically naked save for bits and pieces of neo-Greek get-up. Something about gods and heroes, I got that, but I hadn’t had a chance to look at the program so couldn’t really make out who was who or what was what, aside from knowing that Graham was playing Hecuba and the Trojan War was ending and pretty much everybody was dead. Graham was there alright, an old lady pacing around the stage or sitting on a stool. I suppose the stool was designed by Noguchi, her longtime collaborator. She was rail thin, at least what you could see of her that wasn’t covered by a cape of blackest black, her black dyed hair topped by some kind of golden headdress that matched a golden snake winding up her arm. She wasn’t doing much, just ailing around with her arms and opening her mouth in what was either a pantomime of a shriek or a laugh, I wasn’t sure. I fell into a funk, thinking how much I hate Greek myths and tragedies. For some now incomprehensible reason, I’d enrolled in a semester of Ancient Greek at Berkeley, a nightmare that left me convinced not only that I’d never be able to learn a foreign language but also that I’d never again give a thought to Homer or Sophocles, whose words of wisdom, in pathetic little excerpts, I’d stumbled over in the textbook.

I looked around at our friends, scattered in the front of the orchestra. Ginny seemed mesmerized. Why not? Back in college she had carried around a dog-eared copy of D. H. Lawrence’s The Plumed Serpent, a book that many years ago I dutifully opened only to conclude that it was mythopoetic crap. Ginny had gotten so carried away with the whole southwestern thing that she ended up living on a Navajo reservation for a couple of years. She’s still a sucker for myths and legends, so Cortege of Eagles, whatever the hell it was we were watching, was right up her alley. Mike, a couple of seats past her, was dozing. Smart man. A couple of seats away from him was Jack, the moustachioed cowboy now the moustachioed scholar, whispering in Evelyn’s ear. This isn’t supposed to be about me, but I do wonder why Evelyn never seemed to like me. Still doesn’t. On the rare occasions when I try to talk to her, she looks at me as if I’m something the cat dragged in and dropped on her spotless kitchen floor. What does she have to be so snotty about? Anyway, Evelyn appeared to be listening attentively to Jack, though her eyes remained glued to the stage. Then the applause started. Cortege of Eagles was over. What a relief. Evelyn, clapping respectfully, turned to talk to Jack.

“Honey, get me a champagne,” were the first words out of Marcia’s mouth. “I’ll be with the gang.” To my skeptical raised eyebrow, indicating the overpriced bar and the crush of people no doubt already there, she responded, “Oh, come on, honey, the tickets were free, we’ve gotta support the damn Opera House. And get one for Ginny, too, it’ll help with whatever it is that’s ailing her. She’s got a lot of ailments.” Off I went, though I do hate fighting the line at a bar. Fight I did, then back I came, pleased with myself to be managing the three glasses, handing them around as I arrived to the rat-a-tat-tat of conversation in the circle around Marcia, everybody more or less hanging onto one of the high little bar tables.

“I saw her in the forties,” this was Ginny, “the expression was so pure—it came totally through the body—totally abstract—no mugging, no cheap effects.”

“But can a body be pure?” That was Jack, bringing it around to himself. His drawings of nudes sprawled on the daybed in his studio were up in one of the few good galleries in town. Those drawings were still a little shocking. Some of our friends, who’d assumed that abstract art was all that any longer really mattered, were wondering if Jack’s nudes were radical or retro or if retro was the new radical.

“Well, Jack, your nudes aren’t pure.” That was Mike, his face fixed in his customary half smile, so you weren’t sure if he was being ironic or not.

“They’re certainly not meant to be ironic,” Jack returned, professorial, a little heated.

“Anyway,” Ginny pursued, ignoring the men, “all the mugging and eye rolling, it’s Martha betraying Martha.”

“You don’t like Greek Kabuki?” Mike pressed her, whether mocking or defending Martha it was hard to know. Or was it Ginny he meant to mock, in his laid-back way?

“Greek Kabuki. Right, Mike. That’s it.” This was Marcia. She was winding herself up. “You know what? I think I like the new old Martha better than the old new Martha. Wasn’t there always something fake about that expressive purity of hers? I mean, give me a break. In her dotage she’s let the old thespian dragon who was always in there come out—all the way out. She’s crazed, not with the role but the artifice of the role. Sure it’s schlock. It’s fabulous schlock. Like Sarah Bernhardt on her umpteenth tour, missing a leg or something.”

“Oh, Marcia,” Ginny jumped in, but then fell silent. So did the rest of us. Not that anybody agreed. But Marcia was beginning to sound like Marcia on the page, Marcia in those essays that both excited and infuriated her readers. And talk about schlock, surely there was something if not exactly schlocky then definitely sensationalist about Marcia’s way of eviscerating an artist or an event. Marcia was the higher schlock. Hadn’t Jack said that to Evelyn one night? Hadn’t Mike said it to Jack? Wasn’t Ginny suggesting it right now? There was something carnivalesque about Marcia’s intellectual riffs. But Marcia’s highhandedness could also be seductive. She was so damn definitive. Now she was looking around, assessing the damage, weighing her effect. Her champagne was nearly empty.

“Burt!” She turned to me with a strange look, grabbing my arm, a smidge of champagne dribbling across her dress as her arm flopped down and the plastic glass tipped over. “I better sit down.” She sat, nearly fell backward, onto a banquette, as a woman shoved closer to her husband to make room for Marcia, who was clearly in some kind of distress. And there Marcia was, slumped on the banquette, the plastic glass still gripped in her hand, her eyes rolled back. “Pamela!” It was Mike, turning to the young woman who had been at his side all the time, quiet while we talked. “She’s a doctor,” he explained. Figured. Mike likes competent women; they’re unperturbed when he sends them packing. She ripped open the front of Marcia’s dress, revealing a very expensive-looking lace bra. And began pounding. To no avail. Marcia, who some had predicted at the beginning of the 1960s would be the voice of the decade, author of two nonfiction books, Slummings and A Night at the Opera, dead at forty-five. And, of course, the irony, of the author of A Night at the Opera dying at the Opera House, not lost on the people who wrote the obituaries in The New York Times and the San Francisco Chronicle (where she’d once had a lousy job, so lousy they didn’t even mention it).

item.title: Robert Moor on Rethinking Environmentalism, Tree by Tree
item.content:encoded:
Nonfiction writer Robert Moor joins co-hosts Christian Barter and Jennifer Maritza McCauley to talk about his new book, In Trees, and the power of “tree thinking,” a concept developed by the evolutionary biologist Robert J. O’Hara. Moor explains how this

Nonfiction writer Robert Moor joins co-hosts Christian Barter and Jennifer Maritza McCauley to talk about his new book, In Trees, and the power of “tree thinking,” a concept developed by the evolutionary biologist Robert J. O’Hara. Moor explains how this form of thought emphasizes branching, growth, and pruning, as opposed to hierarchical ordering, and shows how these principles can be identified in the work of writers like Tolstoy and Wordsworth. He explores the role the giant sequoia played in founding modern conservatism and takes listeners on a tour of his own experiences in the trees from Papua New Guinea to Vancouver, Canada, where he participated in a tree sit with activists protesting an oil pipeline. He discusses the ethics of climate activism and how tree thinking might help us re-imagine the environmental movement for a new age. He reads from In Trees.

To hear the full episode, subscribe through iTunes, Google Play, Stitcher, Spotify, or your favorite podcast app (include the forward slashes when searching). You can also listen by streaming from the player below. Check out video versions of our interviews on the Fiction/Non/Fiction Instagram account, the Fiction/Non/Fiction YouTube Channel, and our show website: https://www.fnfpodcast.net/ This podcast is produced by Whitney Terrell.

Robert Moor

In Trees by Robert Moor | Moon Palace Books • On Trails by Robert Moor | Moon Palace Books

Others

The Baron in the Trees by Italo Calvino • “The Trouble with Wilderness” by William Cronon • On the Origin of Species by Charles Darwin • Nature by Ralph Waldo Emerson • How to Blow Up a Pipeline by Andreas Malm • Walden by Henry David Thoreau • Fiction/Non/Fiction Season 9, Episode 56: Matthew Wolfe on the Secret History of Radical Environmentalism

EXCERPT FROM A CONVERSATION WITH ROBERT MOOR

Christian Barter: You have the book divided into tree-related concepts. The chapters are named after branching, pruning, gnarling, rooting, and so on. Your chapter on branching is an especially literary one, and I found it especially thought-provoking. You make a comparison between two writers to demonstrate the difference between narrowing and branching, Wordsworth and Tolstoy. Would you tell us about this comparison and why you chose these two particular writers to make it?

Robert Moor: Yeah. To back up a little bit, the chapter begins when I go to try to climb a tree near my house here where I live, and it is something I’d done as a kid, as you say. I imagine most people do, and then interestingly enough, most people stop for some reason. This tends to be a trend across cultures, and I was sitting there reading actually a book called The Baron in the Trees by Italo Calvino, which you guys have probably read, and thinking about why did I stop climbing trees? You know, it’s a story of a boy who climbs up into a tree and never comes back down, spends his whole life up there.

So I went to climb this tree, and almost right away was seized by this feeling of vertigo, this feeling of cautiousness. You know, it wasn’t just a fear of heights. It was a fear of like, why am I doing something so stupid? I’d lost that kind of wild tree climber’s spirit, and I was feeling that that cautiousness, that narrowness, was kind of infecting other parts of my life, including my writing. I was taking fewer risks. I was sort of falling into a rut that had been carved out. As you know you enter your your 30s and 40s you start to sort of narrow towards the things you’re you’re good at and the things that you are encouraged to do and so I started looking into the neuroscience of this and it some turns out this is actually a fundamental way the brain grows you start out maximally branchy when you are a baby around I believe, the age of two. You have the most neural connections you’ll ever have, and then the rest of your life is spent pruning away those neural connections.

So I became kind of obsessed with the question of staying branchy. This is something that that neuroscientists encourage us to do to to go make sure you’re you’re doing things that are outside of your comfort zone, so that you retain enough of those stray neural connections that you can stay flexible, and you don’t just kind of get winnowed away by by life. And so, going back to your question, this is something that you see very clearly in the life of William Wordsworth. He’s a brilliant poet, of course. He was one of the founders of the English Romantic movement, and really one of the progenitors of the sort of reverence for nature that that many of us have currently.

We are inheritors of his way of seeing the world, but as he got older and as he found success in his life, and as he suffered some personal tragedies, his world and his mind just got narrower and narrower. That’s actually a phrase that I believe Emerson used when he met him. [Wordworth] struck him as a very narrow person, and there are critics who say that if Wordsworth had died at the age of 30, all but one or two of his best poems would still have been written because he really was just on a downward slide from that point. That’s obviously something most of us want to avoid, both the creative narrowness and and the sort of moral narrowness. You know, he lost a lot of the progressive radicalism of his youth, and he became, as many of us do, more and more and more cautious.

So you might assume that this is just a universal thing that we become narrower as we age, and to some degree, it’s true. It’s an unavoidable part of our basic neurology. However, when you look around at other writers, what you find is that some people resist this narrowness. Some people actually become more branchy as they age, or at least they retain enough of that youthful branchiness to really flower into a kind of genius, and that is what I see in the life and the writing of Leo Tolstoy. Tolstoy had this immense interest in life, in all realms of life, including you know gymnastics. Apparently, he taught himself to play tennis in his 70s, and he was swimming in the icy sea, and once got into a fight with a bear and was left with a scar across his face . . . I think the key aspect was he had a really deep regard for and care for other people, especially the powerless, which in Russia at that time would have been the serfs. He said that devotion to helping others was what kind of broke him out of that narrow frame of mind and kept him in a broader, more engaged way of seeing and being in the world.

Jennifer Maritza McCauley: So you also write about how throughout history, trees have been connected to the more spiritual and the more mystical and the more religious ideas and feelings. We were talking a little bit about sequoia trees a little bit earlier. These feelings of awe inspired by sequoia trees led to a material change in environmental policy. Could you just tell us a little bit about sequoias and how their entrance into the public consciousness helped birth the American environmental movement?

RM: Yeah, that’s right. What you see when you sift back through this history, as I did, and and you look at the regard for for trees, if you use trees as a kind of lens for for the environment as a whole, which is a really easy thing to do, I think, because for a lot of us, trees embody the health of the environment. Cutting down a tree is this ultimate symbol of the desecration of the environment, but that wasn’t always the case. I mean, we didn’t always have this very particular reverence for trees that a lot of us have today.

You can [trace that reverence] to people like Wordsworth and people in the German Romantic movement, like Goethe, and then you see how it goes through Emerson and Thoreau and Muir, and it starts to trickle out into the American public, and people start to to raise their voices in saying that trees are really kind of a temple of nature. They help create these sacralized spaces, which it is a desecration to cut down. But the problem was they were up against the forces of capitalism, right? Trees were worth a lot of money. It was really hard to make the argument to the public that you shouldn’t cut them down. And this is true up until the westward expansion in the United States reaches the giant sequoias. The giant sequoias were so unusual; they were so huge and awe-inspiring. [But] their timber was so not valuable. They tended to fall, and their wood would splinter, which made it not great for lumber–as opposed to the coastal redwoods, which are their close cousins. That was very useful timber. They used it for oil pipes and you know railroad ties and all these various things.

Sequoias weren’t like that. So once the environmental movement encounters giant sequoias, suddenly they can use those trees to break the logic of of industrial capitalism, and in fact, there’s a California senator named John Conness who was proposing setting aside the Mariposa [Grove of Giant Sequoias] in what’s now Yosemite National Park, and the other senators are saying to him, There’s no precedent for this. Why would we just set aside a bunch of trees just to stand there and do nothing? And he said, there is no precedent, and there can be no precedent, for there are no other trees on Earth like them, and so from the giant sequoias, I argue, really grows the American conservation movement as a whole.

item.title: On the strange, literary video games of Inpatient Press.
item.content:encoded:
The indie publisher Inpatient Press is doing fascinating, form-breaking work. The small publisher has been putting out fascinating novels, collections, zines and games since 2013. Inpatient’s publisher, Mitch Anzuoni, studied computer science and creative writing in college (fittingly) and aims

The indie publisher Inpatient Press is doing fascinating, form-breaking work. The small publisher has been putting out fascinating novels, collections, zines and games since 2013. Inpatient’s publisher, Mitch Anzuoni, studied computer science and creative writing in college (fittingly) and aims “to publish what others do not.”

Anzuoni told MIT Press, which distributes Inpatient’s book, that “the most important, and perhaps defining, characteristic of my publishing is the treatment of the book as a substantial object on its own, not some ready-made crucible for text and image to be poured into.” This deep interrogation has led to cool experiments in form and distribution, like a series of zines sold via newspaper vending machine. These newsbox offerings (available as a set) included things like Armageddon News, a collection of leaflets and zines created by the FBI to target student activists, alongside their internal communications about this muckraking operation. An interest in the conditions of publication, and its weird slippages and exceptions, runs through everything Inpatient does.

(This isn’t to say they’re not doing “regular” books too—Inpatient has published work by Samuel R. Delaney and Copi, as well as archival projects like a complete reprint of the legendary SF punk zine Search & Destroy.)

Inpatient has also put out games geared more towards a fiction fan than a traditional gamer. Their first and most straightforward game was “Small Press Tycoon”, which is billed as “the original DIY publishing adventure sim.” The game puts you in charge of a small publisher chasing metrics like “hipness” and “quality” as you “print chapbooks and zines, hold readings, discover new and exciting authors, sign distribution deals, and even win industry awards!” It’s all very meta and tongue-in-cheek, blending humor, critique, and surrealism.

This was followed by “Mezzanine,” where you play as an HR administrator at the faux Y2K era multimedia start-up Zentropy. The game’s design is ripped straight from turn-of-the-millennium graphics: Zentropy’s offices are rendered smooth and shiny, approaching a bloated chrome uncanniness. As you explore the empty tech office late at night, sordid secrets are revealed, but the game is most interesting as a knowingly prescient satire of where tech is headed. Or as “Mezzanine”‘s description says, “the lost potential of multimedia and how our current societal psychosis may have always been by design.”

Inpatient’s latest game, “Ex Libris,” came out in April and is perhaps the most literary of the bunch. “Ex Libris” drops you at the entrance to the Abbey of Theleme, a dark, sunken monastery sometime in the mythic Middle Ages. As you make your way past the lo-res ivy and stone lit by the orange glow of firelight, you bump into scattered travelers and locals in the courtyards and chambers: a drunken bookseller, drilling soldiers, a fortune teller and their companion who refuses to speak to you. You also run into lots and lots of books and scrolls, which you can slowly begin to understand as you “learn” the languages they’re written in and translations begin to appear. The moody music, polygonal characters that feel almost hieroglyphic, and text presented in a mix of English, ancient languages, and invented languages make for a hazy experience. The whole game is eerie and mystical.

The exploration is rewarding, and where this starts to feel less like a game and more like literature. As you raise your “logos” stat and begin to “understand” more of the writing and dialogue, the game’s text begins to form a coherence. The writing in the game is quite good, accurately described as an “amalgamation drawing from Umberto Eco, Francois Rabelais, Clark Ashton Smith, Marguerite Porete, and countless other sources to create an interconnected hypercathedral.” I’m not deep enough into the game yet to say definitively what this hypercathedral looks like, but interesting themes about authorship and memory are beginning to emerge, echoed in the game mechanic of discovering hidden archives and unlocking translations.

I found the experience of exploring and reading similar to that of reading a hypertext novel like The Castle of Crossed Destinies or Pale Fire. As you hopscotch through the Abbey, the dislocation begins to fade and the disconnected fragments of text start to form a broader tapestry. Think of “Ex Libris” like if Borges or Cortazar wrote for an old LucasArts point-and-click game.

The writing in “Ex Libris” doesn’t appear to the player as puzzles, or as background texture tacked onto unrelated game mechanics. The pleasure here is not a competitive chase to win or complete the experience. Like a book, “Ex Libris” and Inpatient’s other games aren’t asking us to race up them as a hill to be conquered, but rather to read them based on the narrative, aesthetic, and critical choices made by the author and object itself. In the same sense that you would never say, “I won Helen DeWitt’s latest novel by conquering the various challenges and trials it presented me,” there is no obvious triumph at the end of an Inpatient game. They move non-sequentially in a direction defined by the audience, and getting to choose the frame rate, so to speak, of a book is one of the unique experiences that sets reading apart from other art forms.

But perhaps the gamer “Eyes of pheasant sold at market” said it best in their review of Mezzanine : “You are so lucky that I read alot of books and know what the lacunae are.”

item.title: The Creole Continuum of the Greater Caribbean
item.content:encoded:
The countries of the Greater Caribbean—a region that includes the islands of the Caribbean Sea, the eastern coast of Central America, the southern shores of North America, and the northern coast of South America—are separated by political boundaries and differ in terms of territory, language, and manner of cultural and racial hybridization. The post The Creole Continuum of the Greater Caribbean appeared first on Words Without Borders.

The countries of the Greater Caribbean—a region that includes the islands of the Caribbean Sea, the eastern coast of Central America, the southern shores of North America, and the northern coast of South America—are separated by political boundaries and differ in terms of territory, language, and manner of cultural and racial hybridization. Yet, in the words of Paul Gilroy, they hold in common “shared experiences,” such as historical abduction from Africa, the Middle Passage, and slavery and abolition—experiences that led Antonio Benítez Rojo to coin the term “the repeating island.” From a pan-Caribbean perspective that looks beyond traditional borders and the linguistic legacies of imperialism, this issue aims to present a significant sample of creole literature from the Caribbean Basin. Including stories, poems, novel excerpts, and essays translated from English-, French-, and Spanish-based creoles, our selection seeks to make these languages visible through their own texts, which reveal similarities as well as differences. In addition to translations of Caribbean literature, which can be read alongside the original texts, we include an English-language essay that examines the monument to maroon leader Benkos Biohó in San Basilio, Colombia, as an example of the tensions between memory, history, and liberty in the Palenquero-speaking community.

The “crisis of authority” in European discourse, and the resulting skepticism of monocultural thinking that attended postmodernity, prompted a reassessment of universalist theories and Western epistemic and linguistic paradigms. This changing landscape has given rise to a wealth of new notions of diversity, hybridization, and syncretism that can help to illuminate readings of the postcolonial Caribbean. In its postcolonial discourse, the Caribbean text exemplifies the blending of the colonial past with the new territory in America, which reestablishes the relation to self—a self often worn away by human trafficking. Postcolonial literatures are transcultural, negotiating between various worlds such that ideas of center, purity, essentiality, and authenticity are actively questioned, especially in the linguistic realm.

This issue begins with a text written in a Hispanophone creole. “Catalina Loango” is an oral history transcribed in the illustrated book Chitieno lengua ku ma kuendo: hablemos Palenquero a través del cuento (2011) by Bernarndino Pérez Miranda, an author, translator, educator, and specialist in Spanish-Palenquero bilingualism based in San Basilio de Palenque, Colombia. This is a popular adaptation of a lumbalú or “dance of death” chant that, in a utopian reversal of the Middle Passage, alludes esoterically to the return to Africa, encoded here in the symbolism of the protagonist’s name, “Loango,” which was also the embarkation point for enslaved people departing from the Congo.

Ludmila Ferrari offers further insight into the culture of Palenque with a photo essay that examines the spatial economies of violence through the processes of construction, demolition, and decay in Latin America. In her essay “A Maroon Monument,” she proposes that the representation of freedom in the statue of Benkos Biohó in San Basilio de Palenque, Colombia, is mired in the visual language of slavery and in Western sculptural standards. With time, the inhabitants of Palenque have collectively altered the statue, transforming it into a living space of symbolic dispute. The essay concludes that the maroon monument can be neither monolithic nor stable, but is rather multiple, open, and in constant movement, tied to an experience of liberty that cannot be reduced to the slave-master dichotomy and is instead based in the quotidian, the community, and shared memory.

Also featured in this issue is Emiliana Bernard-Stephenson, a member of the Raizal community from the San Andrés, Providencia, and Santa Catalina islands, and the current Colombian ambassador to Jamaica. She is also known for her work as a journalist, writer, teacher, and feminist. Her poem “Kriol Soldier” demonstrates her commitment to and defense of her mother tongue, San Andrés–Providencia Creole, closely tied to her Raizal identity. The poem reveals the linguistic tension between the English-based creole spoken by the Raizal community and Spanish—imposed since the islands came under Colombian control in the twentieth century—and gestures to the linguistic (and racial) discrimination historically directed at Creole. As an official language of the islands, Spanish exists in diglossia with Creole, which was introduced as an official language of the territory by the Colombian Constitution of 1991—part of a larger movement toward the recognition of ethnic and linguistic diversity within the country.

The award-winning Haitian poet, dramaturg, novelist, and rapper Jean D’Amérique contributes “Poem for Children with Trouble Sleeping,” a mordant take on the political machinery of his country, disguised in the language and rhythm of a lullaby. Through the use of irony, D’Amerique offers us a text that is undermined by its own context, generating a gap between the literal sense of the poem and its true meaning. In this way, the poet draws a harsh contrast between the innocence and vulnerability of the child’s world and the devastating aggression of a state that does not hesitate to use humans as capital.

We are also proud to present the work of Martinican writer Raphaël Confiant, a prolific and multi-award-winning novelist as well as a pioneer in the creole cause. Known for his anticolonial and environmentalist thought, he was also the first Martinican to publish a novel in Creole (Bitako-a, 1985). This book was followed by many others, in both French and Creole, as well as the first dictionary of Martinican Creole. His oeuvre represents the orality of the island and the French-based creole that arose on plantations and remains in use by the Martinican population, coexisting with French, the official and administrative language. In 1989, with Jean Bernabé and Patrick Chamoiseau, Confiant published Éloge de la créolité [In Praise of Creoleness], a foundational defense of Creole identity, language, and culture. Here, we present a sample of his unpublished novel Galfétè Mò (Galfétè is dead), which offers a portrait of the exploitative workings of sugar plantations in Martinique.

Creoles were born as languages of adaptation, and at the same time of resistance. They have long faced stigma, and have only recently been revindicated by the fields of linguistics and postcolonial studies, and by global organizations. One example of this dramatic about-face was the recognition of San Basilio de Palenque, Colombia, as a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO in 2005. Creole literatures are ultimately the supersyncretic result of dialogue between elements arising from African, European, and Asian ethnicities, cultures, languages, and religions; these elements coexist in an oscillating relationship of appropriation and rejection that generates its own new American-born byproducts, such as these creole languages, to whose powerful creative energies this issue is testament.

Works Cited

Paul Gilroy: The Black Atlantic: Modernity and Double-Consciousness, 1993

Antonio Benítez Rojo: The Repeating Island: The Caribbean and the Postmodern Perspective, 1996

Graciela Maglia: De la machina imperial a la vereda tropical. Poesía, identidad y nación en el Caribe Afrohispánico, 2009

Edouard Glissant: Caribbean Discourse, 1999
