item.title: Learning From Shame: R.F. Kuang on Diaspora, Language and Writing Young Protagonists
item.content:encoded:
R.F. Kuang is, in the best sense, a literary chameleon. Each one of her novels presents a different setting and dynamic, but her oeuvre is unified by careful thought, sharp style, and an uncanny ability to make the pages want to turn. Taipei Story, her seventh book since 2018, is about Lily, a college freshman spending a summer abroad in Taiwan to learn Mandarin. She struggles with assimilation, her roommate, Anna, her internet-famous classmate, JC, her self-perception, and the death of her grandfather.

Kuang and I spoke earlier this month—she is as smart in person as she is on the page, funny, insightful, and extremely curious. An edited version of our conversation follows:

*

Adam Dalva: Your book activates so much nostalgia—of course I didn’t have Lily’s exact experience, but I do remember the alienation of being a college student abroad and struggling with both my personal life and a new language. Were you thinking about the way that we look back at this sort of time and say, “Oh my God, what was I doing?”

R.F. Kuang: I was very excited to write a protagonist who was so much younger than me, because up until this point all of my characters have been aging as I age. I started writing the Poppy War trilogy when I was a teenager, and everyone’s a teenager. In Babel, they’re undergrads. In Katabasis, they are PhD students. I just turned 30 this year, and I went back a decade and wrote somebody on the cusp of adulthood. And she’s so book smart, but so amazingly stupid. I found that really fun.

Language is something that is practiced and learned and something that you can be awful at, and also something that you can get better at. But the only way that you get better is by making mistakes.

It’s not from a position of elder arrogance. “I’m 30 now, so I can make fun of the youths.” It’s more being able to let go of a fear of sounding stupid when I’m old enough to see that it really doesn’t matter, that I’d rather make mistakes in public and on the page. When I was a younger writer, I was so nervous about my reader misinterpreting my work or drawing the wrong conclusions about what I believed or my level of expertise, and I tried to show my work on the page. Now I would rather be visibly struggling to learn new material and wrestle with difficult concepts than to be so rigidly attached to an identity of being totally prepared and correct at every turn. Life isn’t an oral exam. I’m messy and the character is messy and we learn a lot more from our mistakes than from received textbook beliefs.

I found it productive to root the narrating voice in somebody for whom the world makes no sense. And the worst part is she thinks she has a grasp on it. She thinks she gets the gist of geopolitics. She thinks she understands the US-Taiwan relationship, the history of mainland China, and the history of Mandarin language education in Taiwan. And she’s just so wrong about everything.

AD: All of that opens so many narrative possibilities for shame and humiliation—and I know from reading your recent Substack essay that shame was one of your interests in this novel.

RK: I think shame and bilingualism go hand-in-hand. Doris Sommer’s Bilingual Aesthetics was instructive for me here. I’m interested in people for whom identity, especially racial, cultural identity, is a card that you play to establish that you have the upper hand, that your word ought to be given more weight. I explored this from a different angle in Yellowface, which is a satire about people making different claims to cultural authority and acting as cultural gatekeepers on the basis of pretty flimsy credentials.

There’s something similar going on with bilingualism. It’s a great source of shame and embarrassment when you don’t have the fluency that your appearance or social position would indicate that you should have. And people also treat their varying levels of fluency as games of one-upmanship. When you go to a Chinese restaurant with a bunch of other Chinese Americans and one of them can just rattle off all the names of dishes on the menu and you can’t even ask for tea, the attitude being signaled is, “Oh, I’m better than you. I’m more Chinese than you. I’m more connected than you.” So a lot of people don’t speak in Chinese because they don’t want to signal, with their accents or poor grammar, that they are less than.

Taipei Story is interested in severing the entitlements of blood or ethnicity from language ability. Language doesn’t come in your blood. Nobody’s born speaking a language. I’m interested in picking apart what the theorist Rey Chow calls the “myth of consanguinity” in her critique of the concept of the “native speaker.” Language is something that is practiced and learned and something that you can be awful at, and also something that you can get better at. But the only way that you get better is by making mistakes.

I’m fascinated in how the language classroom is a daily exercise in shame and humiliation. Those are productive things. The willingness to go in every day and make a total fool of yourself to a room of 10 other people in front of a language teacher who’s actively laughing at you. David Sedaris has a wonderful essay about learning French where he talks about shame almost as a kink. It’s a feeling you grow to enjoy, because unless you were going through that friction, you would be making no progress at all.

AD: I feel very inspired by that as someone who fails at language acquisition of all sorts. And I was thinking about how the final test for learning a language is being casual in a restaurant, whereas the final test, if you’re a student studying Descartes, is an exam about Descartes.

RK: Oh, that’s such a good point. I feel that way, especially in French. I have pretty good reading fluency in French, but almost no speaking ability. And I still wouldn’t dare to order myself breakfast at a Parisian cafe. There’s a moment near the end of the book where Lily is thinking about what acquiring all this Chinese has gotten her, as opposed to playing the guitar or carpentry or woodworking or visual arts. Obviously learning languages is a wonderful thing, but in a different case, particularly for a heritage speaker, it just puts you back at square one amongst all the other people who already speak and live and work in that language.

AD: Taipei Story uses the death of Lily’s grandfather as a counter example of what language can do. I was just reading the Proust sequence where Marcel’s grandmother dies, which is maybe my favorite scene in literature. A grandparent dying is such an intense experience, the repository of family history being lost. And yet the lead has this thought, paraphrasing, that you actually don’t get that much social mileage out of a grandparent dying. So she’s experiencing this deep loss, but the people around her don’t particularly care. And at the same time, she begins to get obsessed with the questions she wishes she could have asked about him about his time in Cambodia. Language would have been a way to cross that divide, but she can’t even go to the funeral. She can just go to the airport to meet her mother for a few hours.

RK: I don’t like being in airports, but I really like airport scenes, especially those in Taiwanese cinema—for instance, the farewell scene in Ang Lee’s The Wedding Banquet really gets me. I was thinking, for people who really exist in multiple cultures, multiple languages, that the flight over is such a strange space where you’re literally caught in the in-between. The flight attendant’s coming down and she’s speaking in both languages and you have to decide which one you want to pick. And so I opened the novel when she’s landing in Taipei Taoyuan Airport. And the emotional peak, the climax, the middle bit with her mother, is these four hours in that liminal space of the airport. And the final scene is her departing and thinking about, as she passes through this portal, if has she really transformed into a different person?

But to answer the question about lost time, I’m working with a fantasy of connection. I think a lot of us, whether or not you’re a part of a diaspora community, experience interactions with grandparents that are tinged with guilt and grief. You’re already mourning their passing and all the conversations that you didn’t have, even while they’re still here. In diaspora communities there’s this fantasy of, “Oh, if I actually did go back, if I did live with them, if I could speak the language, we would have this beautiful connection and they would tell me the truth of everything that they had been through, and I could properly honor that.”

Lily thinks that the only barrier to resolving this fantasy is getting good enough at Chinese, which she doesn’t do in time. But sometimes people don’t want to tell you their stories. Sometimes previous generations think, “That really has nothing to do with you.” She asks her mother, “Why didn’t anybody tell me? This is such a massive traumatic part of our family history; why was I not brought in on this?” And her mother’s just like, “Well, it’s kind of sad, so why would I want to talk about it with you?” And the most charitable way of interpreting that is they lived through all that pain. They fought all those struggles. They escaped everything they did so that Lily, the luckiest generation, doesn’t even have to think about it. For Lily’s grandfather and for her mother, this is a good outcome, the fact that what happened in Cambodia would never cross her mind. But Lily views this as rejection. That involves a lot of assumptions about what we get to be included in and what stories we ought to have access to.

AD: It feeds into something that you’re dealing with in many ways in Taipei Story: expectation versus reality. As with the question of tourism. When I was 19, I actually went to Taipei for a week and I did all the things that Lily does her first week. I looked at the Jadeite Cabbage, I went to Taipei 101, I saw the mass damper. And I was thinking about this beautiful line in Garth Greenwell’s Cleanness where his character goes to Venice and thinks, “I had never cared about important things, their edges were rubbed smooth by too much looking.” As your novel goes along, Lily begins to have rounder experiences in ways that surprise her, ways that might not even be linked to being in Taipei.

I’m working with a fantasy of connection. I think a lot of us, whether or not you’re a part of a diaspora community, experience interactions with grandparents that are tinged with guilt and grief.

RK: When I taught Reading and Writing the Modern Essay, which is one of the undergraduate writing seminars at Yale, the class used the same four units for the first part of the course, but we got leeway to choose our fifth module. I taught travel writing. I started with assigning a provocative New Yorker essay by Agnes Callard, where she argues in part that the expectations that we have when we travel are already so saturated with travel writing and photos that we know the Parthenon from a postcard better than we remember the experience of looking at it. If everything’s been seen and done and all of your experiences aren’t even spontaneous discoveries, if you’re just following a checklist, what are you doing?

And this is complicated in Lily and Anna’s case, because after she and her classmates have formed this little crew, there’s this bizarre pecking order of authority that supposedly has to do with their language level, but really has to do with some silly assumptions about their race. They basically don’t listen to the white kids about where they ought to go, but because Lily and Anna are heritage speakers, although neither of them has ever stepped foot in Taiwan, everybody else looks to them for guidance about what restaurants to go to and what to order and what certain cultural codes mean. Lily is constantly running off to Google things in the bathroom because she feels like she ought to know the answers, but she doesn’t.

This wrinkle of being a heritage tourist comes up again when Lily’s thinking about a Jamaica Kincaid essay that she was assigned—that’s the first part of A Small Place, which really has nothing to do with Lily’s situation at all—and it’s another symptom of Lily’s need to make everything that ever happened in the history of the world about her. When she’s thinking about Kincaid’s reflections on British tourists, she wonders, “but ethically, does that implicate me? Are we in a similar situation just because I’m American? Does that make me so bad?” And it’s just a very undergraduate, torturous, navel-gazing question about whether every interaction is already colored by expectation and a tourism industry, and in this case, the long history of foreign language programs as soft power, which is just the tip of a massive geopolitical historical iceberg.

AD: I was fascinated by the way you write about gossip in this book, and it feeds into what we’re talking about with how we construct identity. When we’re in an airplane going to a place, we can say, “I’m going to take on a new self. This is who I’m going to be now.” But then gossip can sometimes circulate and trap someone. You have this wonderful character, JC, who at first readers might feel is going to be a love interest. And then it turns into something pretty nefarious.

RK: I had so much fun writing the interactions between Lily and JC. I guess a place to start is that I wanted to write a book without a bad guy. You use the word nefarious, but there’s not actually any malice involved. It’s a lot of miscommunication. And I don’t really think JC does anything wrong. He does things that are extremely immature, but none of it is motivated by an actual desire to hurt Lily. And I feel that very little of the gossip as it spreads through her program is motivated by a desire to hurt Lily either. Lily’s revelations at the end of the book take the form of, “Oh wait, it really wasn’t as bad as I thought.” I think the gossip hits Lily very hard because she feels the back of her neck prickle because she thinks everybody’s looking at her. And she’s not wrong. But it doesn’t take the form of this social ostracization ala an Edith Wharton novel. She assigned that pariah status to herself and decides, “I have to be completely alone for the last few weeks of my time in Taipei.” And so it’s less about the insidious nature of perceptions or bout Lily being frozen into an image against her will, and more about adolescents disproportionately assigning stakes to things.

AD: We both teach. I went to college a while ago, but I still remember all my teachers. I can tell you pretty much beat-for-beat what happened in junior year Japanese literature classes. And yet if I went to see that professor, he would have no idea who I am. This idea of disproportionate experience comes up for me as a teacher, the thought that there might be a student in the corner who doesn’t really talk, and I don’t think about them very much, but probably 15 years later, they’ll still have a memory of my class, whereas I am statistically likely to not remember them at all.

RK: I’m going to start my first position as a professor in the fall, but I’ve been teaching as a grad student for a couple of years. And the first few cohorts I had, within the first three weeks, I knew everybody’s names, knew their stories, and I really thought, “I’m going to remember these kids for the rest of my life.” I got used to the sound of their writing and had a personal investment in all of their arcs. But there was a moment this past spring where I was thinking about a class from just that previous fall and I was like, “I don’t know their names.” I can think of some of their faces, but it’s like I completely memory holed them after I turned in their final grades.

I don’t think that diminishes my investment in them as instructor, but there’s one of me and 15 of them. And I think probably there are always going to be some standout students, but no matter how positive an experience we have, I just don’t think about them that much, and maybe they’ll think about me a lot more. And it’s particularly complicated in the case of language instructors, because to loop back to what I was saying about shame and humiliation, I think we form an attachment to language instructors, especially if you’re heritage students, that are very necessary. I’m sure you could do a lot with this with psychoanalysis and stuff about transference and attachment. I found Merve Emre’s essay “Are You My Mother?” especially helpful on this. There’s this parental projection for Lily. And I think a lot of heritage speakers feel that way, because they might’ve come from context where most of the people that they ever spoke that language around was a family member.

When I was in Taiwan, I was taking classes and I just kept thinking, “You’re not my mom. You’re not my mom. You’re not my aunt.” But there was some buried, unconscious part of me that kept feeling this way. And Lily has shared so much with her one-on-one teacher. She has cried in the classroom. She has admitted very vulnerable things. She’s really dug deep into herself and offered herself up raw and hurting and struggling. And so I wanted to include that image near the end of the semester, or the end of term, where her teacher’s scrolling through all the folders to get to Lily’s essay. And she’s like, “Oh, shit. I’m a folder to her.” And you just have to accept that as a student, otherwise you’re being weird.

item.title: What Weimar Berlin’s Most Famous Plays Revealed About Artistic Freedom
item.content:encoded:
Is there a German word that means the opposite of “doppelgänger”—not the uncannily mysterious twin, but the secretly matched-up opponent who stands for everything one hates and also hates everything one stands for? If so, Bertolt Brecht could have filled that role for Vladimir Nabokov. It would be hard to imagine two more dissimilar writers inhabiting the same city at the same time. While Nabokov was yearning toward a lost aristocratic past, Brecht was actively championing a proletarian future in which the downtrodden would finally triumph over their exploiters. And where Nabokov kept his politics (if he had any) well under wraps, Brecht wore his on his sleeve—or rather, on signboards thrust in the faces of his audiences.

Brecht, born in Augsburg in 1898, was only a year older than Nabokov, so they were about the same age during those two decisive events of their youth, the Great War and the Russian Revolution. For Nabokov, the former was an important piece of history occurring mainly at a distance while the latter was a permanent tragedy; for Brecht, the situation was almost exactly reversed. Though he never became an official Party member, Brecht was known to sympathize with the Soviet revolutionary cause, and he was to manifest those class sympathies in most of his writing. Still, his left-wing politics did not prevent him from concerning himself with aesthetic matters as well. Like Nabokov, he started out mainly as a writer of poetry, and in the end, ironically, his lifelong efforts in that direction turned out to be much more meaningful for German literature than Nabokov’s early poetic forays were for the Russians.

But it was not as a poet that Brecht came to be known, either in the Berlin of his time or in the wider world. His fate was to be celebrated as a playwright and theatrical collaborator, at first with the dramaturgical innovator Erwin Piscator and then with the composer Kurt Weill. In particular, Brecht’s instantaneous fame arrived shortly after he turned thirty, when his second or third collaboration with Weill, The Threepenny Opera, opened at the Theater am Schiffbauerdamm on August 31, 1928.

The work’s profound effect on the world that came after it…has been so far-reaching as to obliterate any possibility of seeing or hearing it afresh.

Though some critics and a few audience members were initially taken aback by this odd hybrid—neither opera nor play, neither high art nor cheap entertainment, neither satire nor straight political commentary, but a kind of weird combination of all of them—the production was soon recognized as a major hit. In his capacity as the Berliner Zeitung am Mittag’s cultural reporter, Billie Wilder published a column on October 22, 1928, about visiting The Threepenny Opera’s fiftieth performance, where he observed that the “opera’s enduring appeal owes to a fusion of outrageous wit and social criticism.” He pointed out, correctly, that “Kurt Weill’s music is a large part of that appeal,” and concluded by saying: “There was as much applause for this fiftieth performance as there had been for the first.”

About a month earlier, the aesthetically choosy Count Harry Kessler had also attended the show. “In the evening saw Brecht’s Dreigroschenoper, music by Weill,” he wrote in his diary entry for September 27. “A fascinating production, with rudimentary staging in the Piscator manner and proletarian emphasis (apache style). Weill’s music is catchy and expressive and the players (Harald Paulsen, Rosa Valetti, and so on) are excellent. It is the show of the season, always sold out.”

Later that fall, at a big party given at Piscator’s apartment—an “attractive, bright flat, designed by Gropius,” Kessler can’t help mentioning—he meets the playwright himself. “I was introduced to Brecht,” he notes in his October 30, 1928, diary entry. “Strikingly degenerate look, almost a criminal physiognomy, black hair and eyes, dark-skinned, a peculiarly suspicious expression; very nearly a typical twister. But in conversation he thaws and comes within an ace of being naïve. I told him, apparently to his great delight, stories about d’Annunzio. Superficially, at any rate, he has a head on his shoulders.” Despite that final note of praise, one would hardly have expected the snobbish count to further his acquaintance with the self-styled proletarian playwright, and indeed he did not.

It’s hard to define from a distance exactly what was so special about those early performances of The Threepenny Opera. This is true of any live production, of course, but in this case the problem is exacerbated by history. The work’s profound effect on the world that came after it, in everything from theater to jazz to graphic art to film to television commercials, has been so far-reaching as to obliterate any possibility of seeing or hearing it afresh.

Even in its time, it was viewed as both highly original and an acknowledged copy. Loosely adapted from John Gay’s The Beggar’s Opera, the story is set in an imaginary London inhabited by English-named figures like Peachum, Brown, and Macheath. All the characters are, to one extent or another, criminals (perhaps this was why Kessler associated Brecht’s appearance with them); even the cops are criminals, and in fact the sheriff may be the most corrupt figure of all. The play’s main character, Mack the Knife, is simultaneously attractive and repulsive, and the role works best when neither of those two sides is neglected. That Brecht identified with his imperfect hero can be deduced, perhaps, from the fact that in 1929 he was taped singing Mack’s theme song, “Die Moritat von Mackie Messer,” in a pitch-perfect two-minute recording. Or maybe what this demonstrates is that by 1929 the song was so famous that even a non-singing author could make a hit out of it. The Weill score, as everyone pointed out, was brilliant, ranging as it did from honky-tonk brassiness to delicate sentimentalism, all with a minor-key tang that gave a fresh memorability to every phrase.

In the first year after its premiere, The Threepenny Opera was performed over three hundred times at the Schiffbauerdamm alone, with another four thousand or so performances taking place at theaters throughout Europe. Still, nothing lasts forever, and by the summer of 1929 the management of the Theater am Schiffbauerdamm was ready for another play. And who better to come up with it than Bertolt Brecht and Kurt Weill?

Happy End, their first collaboration after The Threepenny Opera, opened on September 2, 1929, and ran for less than a week. It was a disaster, both financially and aesthetically. No doubt this can be traced back to numerous flaws, but the main one is that the later opera was just a pale copy of its predecessor. It was set among criminal types in Chicago rather than London, but with similarly lovable/hateful characters presented in a similarly sardonic mode. Worst of all, the songs in Happy End, when they were not just dull and repetitive, tended to sound like faint imitations of Threepenny’s best melodies. Both “Surabaya Johnny” and “The Bilbao Song,” for instance, featured many of the same chord progressions and rhythmic strategies that Weill had already used in “Pirate Jenny” (memorably sung in The Threepenny Opera by Lotte Lenya, the composer’s wife). And whereas audiences had loved these musical phrases the first time around, they didn’t need to hear them again so soon, especially in recycled form.

*

Meanwhile, over at Piscator’s rival theater on Nollendorfplatz, something entirely new was happening. Only four or five years older than Brecht, Erwin Piscator had been a major force in the development of the Weimar era’s “epic theater,” the dramatic form which Brecht ultimately took over as his own. Piscator, who practiced his art primarily as a stage manager and director rather than a writer (though he did publish a 1929 book called The Political Theatre), was known as one of Berlin’s cutting-edge theatrical collaborators. He had worked with Brecht and Weill as recently as 1928, involving Brecht in the adaptation of The Good Soldier Schweik and getting Weill to write incidental stage music for Leo Lania’s play Oil Boom, both of which Piscator directed at his own recently founded theater, Piscator-Bühne. Now, however, he drew on a new pair of collaborators—Moholy-Nagy for the set design, Hanns Eisler as the song composer—to help him usher in a new play by Walter Mehring called The Merchant of Berlin.

Mehring, a Berliner born and raised, had built a reputation mainly as a satirist, a poet, and a lyricist responsible for cabaret songs. A declared anarchist and Dadaist, he published many of his short pieces in left-wing papers and magazines like Das Tagebuch and Weltbühne. He was friends with the painter Georg Grosz and, like Grosz, he had a somewhat ambivalent attitude toward the New Objectivity’s advocacy of realism. On the one hand, these two artists supported the need to portray the conditions of life among the disenfranchised and to make a case for the unfairly oppressed. On the other hand, they wanted the freedom to depart from reality into the satiric and the metaphorical. As Grosz put it when speaking with Harry Kessler (in a conversation that took place at that same party where Kessler first met Brecht), “Reality as such does not interest me…what I aspire to is the fabulous. The camera can achieve all sorts of interesting snippets, but never the magical effects of draughtsmanship.” In his own medium—words—Mehring seems to have been aspiring to the same sort of thing.

This was shocking, but of course it was meant to be. And where did one draw the line, anyway, between allowable excess and disruptive public discourse?

Der Kaufmann von Berlin self-consciously alluded, in its title and to a certain extent its plot, to Shakespeare’s Merchant of Venice. It is an echo that any educated German would have heard, because Shakespeare had long since been claimed by Germany as one of its own: Schlegel’s nineteenth-century translations, some Germans insisted, were so good as to transcend the originals. In Mehring’s redone version of the tale, an Eastern European Jew named Kaftan arrives in Berlin in 1923 with only a hundred dollars in his pocket and quickly turns himself into a millionaire by taking advantage of inflation. Like Shylock with his Jessica, Kaftan has a daughter named Jessi whom he adores. Like Shylock, Kaftan is persuaded by a Gentile into making an unwise and ultimately dangerous investment. But unlike Shylock—a fully formed, exceedingly complicated character capable of generating both disgust and sympathy from an audience—Kaftan is more like a caricature, or at any rate a type, intended to represent the whole category of shtetl Jews. Gullible almost to the point of stupidity, easily put upon by the demands and enticements of others, he is the object of nearly unceasing antisemitism, not just as practiced by the Gentiles who trick him, but also on the part of the assimilated Jews he meets in Berlin. In this sense, Mehring’s play is echoing Einstein’s critique of the wealthy German Jews who disdained their poorer Eastern cousins.

The plot hovers between the fantastical and the realistic. The severe inflation of 1923 and the rise of the nationalist movement are portrayed in their true colors, but both the degree of profiteering and the engineering of right-wing coups are exaggerated for effect. Mehring’s characters include petty criminals, unscrupulous lawyers, Galician Jews, Freikorps heavies, local and international businessmen, Prussian generals, and the everyday citizens inhabiting the streets of Berlin’s old and rather dingy center. Nobody comes off well; if anything, the snooty German Jews almost seem more vicious than the right-wing plotters, who are presented as mercenary and power-hungry rather than ideological.

The script itself is filled with the language of its time and place, including Berliner gutter slang and high-society clichés, casino speech and capitalist jargon, spoken Yiddish and literary German. The Yiddish is actually so prevalent, especially in the dialogues between Kaftan and his daughter, that it’s not clear a normal German theater audience could have understood those parts. The daughter, incidentally, is a tuberculosis patient in a Swiss sanatorium (shades of Thomas Mann’s Magic Mountain, which had appeared to great acclaim only five years earlier). Her medical fate is used by Kaftan’s deceivers to lure him into their trap, though again, this potential source of human feeling receives no emotional support from Mehring’s satiric style.

For Mehring—who was himself a Jew, though never a practicing one—The Merchant of Berlin may have been a way of writing about antisemitism, not only as a wider societal problem but also as it manifested itself within the Jewish community of Berlin. For Piscator, who came at it from a strongly Marxist perspective, the play was essentially about class. Presenting the work on a four-level stage that stratified the different elements of society, he emphasized the role of the cash nexus in undermining human relations. Not that he had to contort the script to do so, for Mehring purposely sets his work in 1923 to highlight the instability caused by extreme inflation. In a period when cash itself has no fixed value, everyone’s status is at risk: even the rich, whose money normally insulates them, find themselves floundering in quicksand, unsure from one moment to the next when they might be sucked under. That Kaftan happens to own American dollars rather than German currency turns out to be crucial to his success, though he only realizes this after naïvely showing off his money in a pub in order to get service from the antisemitic owner.

When the work premiered on September 6, 1929, the scandal it caused was immediate and substantial. Mehring was accused in different newspapers of promoting both pro-Jewish agitation and antisemitic hate speech. Under Joseph Goebbels’ guidance, the paramilitary Sturmabteilung—the storm-troopers, otherwise known as the SA—held a massive protest in front of the theater. In addition, Goebbels wrote and distributed a pamphlet called “To the gallows!” that explicitly attacked Mehring and his play. And despite some subdued and possibly mixed defenses offered by other Berlin writers (one of his fellow satirists, Kurt Tucholsky, praised him as “the first plane over Berlin”), Mehring ultimately considered it necessary to leave Germany, first for Paris and then for Vienna.

The Goebbels pamphlet issued on this occasion seems to have disappeared, but another of his 1929 screeds, published under the satiric title “Those Damn Nazis,” can provide something of its flavor. “The Jew is the cause and beneficiary of our slavery. He has misused the social misery of the broad masses to deepen the dreadful split between right and left of our people,” Goebbels wrote. “The Jew caused our problems, and lives from them…He has ruined our race, corrupted our morals, hollowed out our customs and broken our strength…Where he finds filth and decay, he surfaces and begins his butcher’s work among the nations…The Jew is uncreative. He produces nothing, he only haggles with products…He has somehow stolen everything he deals in.” At one point, as if harking back to Shakespeare, the pamphleteer seems to answer Shylock’s despairing “Hath not a Jew eyes?” by admitting that “the Jew, after all, is a human being. Certainly, none of us doubts that.” But having conceded this much, he then takes it back: “We only doubt that he is a decent human being…If someone slaps your mother in the face, do you say: ‘Thank you! He is after all a human being!’ That is not a human being, it is a monster. Yet how much worse has the Jew done to our mother Germany, and is still doing today!”

This was shocking, but of course it was meant to be. And where did one draw the line, anyway, between allowable excess and disruptive public discourse? In early September of 1929, things still appeared sufficiently stable, both economically and politically, for this kind of theater-driven scandal to be viewed as just another aspect of the edgy Berlin atmosphere. Yes, Goebbels’ language was certainly hateful, but no thinking person read such stuff. And true, the street demonstrations were sometimes frightening, if you happened to be in the wrong place at the wrong time. But were the majority of Berlin’s citizens worried about what all this might mean in the long run? Did they think Mehring’s fantastical and exaggerated vision of antisemitic, corruption-driven political coups could ever become a reality? Not a chance.

_______________________________

From Berlin Before and After: A Cautionary Mirror for Our Times by Wendy Lesser. Copyright © 2026 by Wendy Lesser. Reprinted by permission of HarperCollins Publishers.

item.title: What Peatlands Can Teach Us About Time
item.content:encoded:
I am sitting in a frost pocket in West Virginia, looking at a Canada warbler.

It is World Migratory Bird Day in spring, the second Saturday of May, and I have spent the past week in search of warblers. The Appalachian Mountains roll out a green carpet for songbirds making their annual migration between the winter warmth of Central and South America and the northern habitats they need to breed and nest. Some birds will pass through and continue on to the boreal forests of Canada; this warbler might be one of them. Some birds find their sweet spot along the 2,000 miles of mountain ridges that flow southwest to northeast. Their route traces the compressed, parallel spines of ancient rock, a corrugated topography of knobs and hollers. As the land dips and rises, these small travelers find their comfort zone in the microclimate and plant communities that suit them best.

I have a moment of spatial and temporal dislocation: I could be much farther north, or I could be watching a landscape emerging from the last ice age.

To follow the birds, I follow the geography, which led me to the Cranberry Glades Botanical Area, a peatland nestled in the Monongahela National Forest.  The protected area encompasses an assemblage of peat bogs that resemble the muskegs of northern Canada. At 3,400 feet in the Allegheny Mountains, the Glades exist in a place where cold air sinks from the surrounding mountain slopes into low hollows—aptly called frost pockets. These pockets create the climate conditions that sustain plant species more commonly found in the boreal north, survivors from colder times long past. This dense, wet habitat is where the Canada warblers feel at home.

The Glades are warming up to spring, still swathed in dried sedges from last fall. The word “glade” comes from Middle English, or Old English “gloed,” meaning a bright, sunny place, a clearing in a forest. I enter a boardwalk that makes a looping path along the edge of Round Glade, through a dense patch of alders and giant rhododendron, and past a corner of Flag Glade. The wooden walkway is weathered and warped; unlike elevated boardwalks in other peatlands I’ve visited, this one sits nestled directly on the uneven terrain of the bog. The Glades are lush with Sphagnum mosses, black chokeberry, skunk cabbage, and a creeping mat of teaberry. Cinnamon ferns form hummocks, with tightly wound fiddleheads stretching upwards toward the sun, just beginning to unfurl into emerald fronds. The deep-red, leathery leaves of northern pitcher plant emerge from the moss, rising below the dried flower heads from last summer.

I watch the Canada warbler flit from branch to branch in a red spruce (Picea rubens), another species of colder climes. Red spruce forests once covered a million acres of the central Appalachians, before being reduced by logging, fire, acid rain, and wind damage from the loss of sheltering trees. An estimated 10 to 20 percent of red spruce forests remain in these mountains, though they are slowly increasing through extensive tree-planting and restoration efforts.

The warbler flies to an eastern hemlock. It sees me too, with its bright eye encircled by a bold white ring. This male bird’s lemon-yellow underside is adorned with fine black streaks that form a necklace across its breast. I sit still and listen to bird song in a dozen languages and the soft breath of wind through the fresh green leaves of alders. I have a moment of spatial and temporal dislocation: I could be much farther north, or I could be watching a landscape emerging from the last ice age.

The Cranberry Glades is a relict from another time, formed more than 10,000 years ago. Like many peatlands in the northern latitudes, the Glades developed as the last glacial period waned and the earth became warmer and wetter. There have been many ice ages in the planet’s history, but it is the Pleistocene that captures our interest because it coincides with the story of human expansion across the globe. People were part of Pleistocene history, adapting to the colder climates in the north and traversing the unglaciated regions to the south of the glacial margins. My distant ancestors may have stood on a hill looking across a half-frozen landscape.

Healthy peatlands represent massive carbon sinks.

To understand peatlands requires thinking on a much longer timescale than the life of a human. Peatlands are ancient habitats whose histories are measured in millennia rather than decades or centuries. The process of building a peatland is slow, almost incomparable to our own experience: in the time it takes for a person to be born, grow up, and grow old, a peatland might have deepened by just a few inches.

Peatlands are wetlands that are proficient in accumulating organic matter, preserving the bounty of life and death in layers of watery peat. Peat becomes a kind of time capsule; core samples taken from deep peats reveal the story of the peatland’s past lives. As the process of decay in the saturated and acidic peat slows to a glacial pace (no pun intended), leaves, seeds, and pollen are captured whole or in fragments. Scientists examining these core samples can identify the kinds of plants that filled the peatland and reveal changes in environmental conditions that occurred over time. The organic matter in peat is more than historic evidence: it is a carbon treasure chest.

Plants, like all life forms in our world, are carbon-based. The carbon dioxide they absorb through photosynthesis is transformed into plant tissue, and when plants die, much of that stored carbon is recycled back into the soil and the air. The carbon cycle never stops, but in peatlands, it slows down considerably. This capacity to hold carbon in the ground is what gives peatlands significant influence in the earth’s climate system.

Healthy peatlands represent massive carbon sinks. An often-quoted fact about peatlands is that they cover only about 3 or 4 percent of the land surface, yet they store twice as much carbon as all the world’s forests combined. But peatlands that are damaged—by drainage, fire, or a warming climate—can release that stored carbon back into the atmosphere, contributing to the concentration of greenhouse gases that is driving climate change.

What happens to carbon under our feet is part of an even longer story, one that dives deeper into the earth and further back in time. Some 350 million years ago, the Carboniferous Period was a fecund era in the planet’s history; plant life was abundant and the earth was warm and wet. Lush forests of giant club mosses and ferns produced bountiful quantities of organic matter. As plants died and were buried in the mud, they formed deep layers of peat. With the right ingredients—time, heat, pressure—the process of carbonization transformed organic material (peat) into a solid form of carbon, and thus, coal was born.

The full story is, of course, more complicated: rising and falling of sea levels, cycles of flooding and burial of peat, and pressure from tectonic shifts in the ancient Pangea supercontinent. The combination of these forces ultimately produced massive coal seams that fueled the Industrial Revolution. Some of these coal beds run through the mountains of West Virginia—not far, in fact, from where I am standing. West Virginia is the largest producer of bituminous coal in the US, with active coal mines in almost half of its 55 counties. In 2025, the state produced 86 million short tons of coal, an increase of 8 percent from the previous year.

While coal production in the US has been in decline for almost two decades, there is still plenty of coal left to be mined. A map of West Virginia’s remaining coal reserves shows a swath running diagonally through the state containing an estimated 1.6 trillion tons.

Here is where the threads of time and human history come together in a tangled knot. Peatlands absorb carbon from the atmosphere and store it, effectively, for millennia. Coal, the product of millions of years of carbon buried under pressure and heat, has an even longer history. When this buried carbon is unearthed and released back to the atmosphere, the climate system responds: carbon dioxide and methane are powerful greenhouse gases that warm the planet. The carbon cycle is spinning wildly, as the carbon accumulated over vast stretches of time is recycled in a flash. Peatlands and coal beds have one thing in common: left undisturbed, they can keep carbon locked in the ground.

If I count time looking backwards, I see myself as a recent arrival, a member of Homo sapiens that appeared perhaps 300,000 years ago. The Canada warbler, singing from its hidden perch, hails from a species that evolved one or two million years ago. The Sphagnum mosses that surround me arose some 14 million years ago, the descendants of mosses that evolved 400 million years ago, making their lineage older than the coal seams that runs through the deep mountains. What if I were to count time looking forward, imagining this scene in a thousand or ten thousand years? Will the deep hollows be moist with mosses, shaded by red spruce and hemlock? Will the air hum with birds and insects?

The rhythm of a bird’s life is measured in seasons. Mine is in years, which seem to be accumulating all too quickly. The peatland around me records its time over millennia. Walking along the boardwalk through the Glades, I feel the lure of falling back into the past. How far would I want to go? Before the invention of the internal combustion engine, perhaps. Not as far back as the last ice age. I savor the peace and quiet in this pocket of peatland, and feel grateful I am here, in the present.

__________________________________

Water, Carbon, Time by Jennifer de Mooy is available from the University of Minnesota Press.

item.title: “Get Out.” Advice on Teaching High School From the Late, Great Frank McCourt
item.content:encoded:
On my second day as a rookie English teacher at my alma mater, Stuyvesant High School, I walked down the fourth floor hallway on my way to class.

Behind a thick column, lurking in the shadows, a kind looking man with an Irish brogue quietly summoned me. “Psst…hey, come over here.”

When I strolled over, he blurted out: “Get out while you can!”

He saw my quizzical expression, not quite comprehending his warning.

“It’s five shows a day, in front of the toughest audience you’ll ever face,” he said with a twinkle in his eye.

The man was Frank McCourt, Stuyvesant’s venerated creative writing teacher. I was immediately smitten.

Thus began the most rewarding mentorship and friendship that I’ve ever had. Two years later, I heeded his advice and “got out” to pursue my dream of a journalism career. Even after I left teaching, we stayed close, and our lives continued to intersect.

A few days after his first essay appeared in print, an excited Frank called me from a phone booth on East Ninth Street, near the pub. His voice sounded electric.

Frank clearly was a highly adored teacher but that wasn’t his ultimate dream—he really wanted to make it as a writer. But no path had yet opened for him, and he was in his late fifties. I recall one day the famous Jerzy Kosinski, author of Being There and The Painted Bird, came to speak at Stuyvesant, and after his remarks, Frank went up to him and plaintively asked: “How can I be a writer like you?”

He told me a few times when we were teaching together that on nights and weekends he was trying to write a book about his impoverished childhood, but he “couldn’t get the sounds of the classroom” out of his ears.

I left Stuyvesant because I was offered a job as Editor of a new weekly newspaper covering the West Side of Manhattan. It was a great first journalism job, and I was only 24. Frank told me he was proud that I was chasing my dream.

About a year after I left teaching, Frank and I had one of our occasional dinners at the Lion’s Head restaurant on Christopher Street in Manhattan. It was a well-known journalist and author hang out. That night, we eyed revered columnist Pete Hamill across the bar. Frank told me he was jealous of Hamill and Jimmy Breslin, two of the more literary columnists who became famous in New York in the 1980s.

Frank took his eyes off Hamill and turned to me, a pint in his hands, and said: “You know, I’ve always wanted to be a columnist.”

“Interesting. What would you want to write about?” I asked, playing along.

“Well, one week I’d go to a pub, and I’d observe whether the bartender mixed good drinks and if there was a lively conversation at the bar. The next week, I’d go to a church or synagogue, and I’d review the rabbi or preacher’s sermon. And the next week, I’d go to a school and sit in on a few classes and write about whether the teachers in that school were really engaging the kids.”

I nodded my head and said: “Hmm… that could be interesting.”

“They’re the three most important institutions in society—pubs, houses of worship and schools—and nobody writes about them unless there’s a scandal,” Frank elaborated.

Two weeks later, a new monthly column by Frank McCourt, called “Forays,” appeared in The West Side Spirit.

The debut piece was a witty, literary look at the history and enduring appeal of McSorley’s, a pub on East Seventh Street in Manhattan. The city’s oldest drinking establishment, it opened its doors in 1854, and it continues to serve up ales and stouts even today, 172 years later. It was Frank’s favorite watering hole.

But halfway through our journey, we hit an unexpected roadblock: You can’t name a school after a living person.

A few days after his first essay appeared in print, an excited Frank called me from a phone booth on East Ninth Street, near the pub. His voice sounded electric.

“Tom, you won’t believe what I just saw. Hanging above the men’s urinal is a framed copy of my McSorley’s column. Do you know how many people will see that?!!!”

Years later, after Angela’s Ashes became a worldwide phenomenon and sold more than 10 million copies, I’d introduce Frank at an annual event he emceed for my media company, called “The Blackboard Awards.” We honored 25 Teachers of the Year in New York City, and the assembled crowd was always enthralled by Frank’s entertaining storytelling and commentary.

In my introduction of him those evenings, I’d tell the McSorley’s bathroom urinal story. “Until he wrote Angela’s Ashes, that was Frank’s best-read piece of writing,” I’d deadpan, as the whole audience broke into laughter.

I was so proud that Frank and I ultimately chased our individual dreams. For him it meant overnight worldwide fame, albeit after years of trying to write. He was always a bit shocked by all the attention. He once said of the hoopla: “Tom, I’m the mick of the moment.” And he’d flash his impish grin.

I knew while I was editing his essays that he was a singular talent—literary, profane, wise, cutting, and unique all at once. His prose would crackle off the page as if to say: “LISTEN! This is important!”

I was excited to showcase his talents and allow him to see that he belonged in New York’s journalism ecosystem. He was painstaking in writing those pieces and it showed in his final drafts. They required very little editing. Why mess with a future Pulitzer Prize winner?

Watching Frank teach, as I did as often as I could, was like watching a master on stage. He knew how to lob provocative questions at his students, elicit more detail from monosyllabic answers all while making learning joyful. His assignments were genius: “Go home and write a restaurant review of your mother (or father’s) home cooked dinner tonight. Lots of detail. I want to SMELL the pasta when I’m done reading it.”

Or: “Go home and write the most creative excuse note you can for why you didn’t do last night’s homework. Most creative one doesn’t have to do homework for two weeks.”

After Frank passed away in 2008, The New York Times posted his lengthy obituary online. I noticed a few thousand comments posted in the first week, most of them former students singing his praises and reminiscing about how his class turned them on to writing.

He had students, like Susan Gilman, who went on to become successful memoirists and novelists. Gilman once told me that Frank saved her life: as a brooding 16-year-old she found purpose in his creative writing class. His attention gave her the hunger to become a great writer to make him proud—and he was.

After Frank’s searing memoir captured the minds of millions around the planet and he won numerous awards, I would gleefully watch his well-earned fame. And between book tours and lectures and television interviews, we would periodically catch up. One day he called for advice: “We’re buying this co-op on West 77th Street. What is this thing, a co-op board interview?”

This was Frank’s first foray into New York’s cutthroat real estate market. “Just be yourself at the interview and they’ll fall for you like I did more than a decade ago,” I said.

In 2008, as a publisher and education activist, I was given the opportunity to help create a new public high school on West 83rd Street with local Council member Gale Brewer, a West Side legend.

At the teacher awards ceremony that Frank emceed for my company, he’d always lament that schools are never named after teachers—just politicians or astronauts or other undeserving people.

Remembering Frank’s words, I suggested to Brewer that we name the new school after Frank McCourt, an immigrant success story that would inspire kids of all backgrounds. Coming to New York penniless, he worked odd jobs to survive before embarking on a high school teaching career of two decades before he wrote one of the most beloved books of the late 20th century, Angela’s Ashes.

Gale liked my idea, and we embarked on getting community buy-in to create a school focused on creative writing. But halfway through our journey, we hit an unexpected roadblock: You can’t name a school after a living person.

I had to call Frank about the problem. “Don’t worry, Frank, we will figure out a way around this,” I said, trying to convince myself and him that all would be ok.

I realized that Frank and I had a great friendship—seeing each other through good times and bad, coaching each other on professional aspirations and ultimately becoming inextricably linked by our shared pasts.

I’ll never forget his response, which even as I type this, sends a chill down my spine. “Well, I guess I better hurry up then.”

A week later, I found out that Frank had passed out on a cruise and that led to a revelation that he was very ill. I couldn’t believe it. It made my passion for creating this school accelerate.

Frank passed away in July 2009. That summer I worked day and night campaigning for Frank McCourt High School. At his memorial service in early September, I got on stage with Frank’s wife, Ellen, and NY City’s Schools Chancellor, Joel Klein, and we announced that Frank McCourt high school would open that Fall. I stood on stage with a bittersweet feeling: I already missed Frank, but I was glad I was able to help make his dream come true. In his final weeks, I gave him updates on the school’s progress, and he seemed very pleased.

I realized that Frank and I had a great friendship—seeing each other through good times and bad, coaching each other on professional aspirations and ultimately becoming inextricably linked by our shared pasts.

__________________________________

Sez I to Myself: The Collected Essays of Frank & Malachy McCourt edited by Tom and Jonah Allon is available from Abrams.

item.title: Read the Winners of American Short Fiction’s 2026 Insider Prize
item.content:encoded:
Writing is a challenge, at every level. There are constant pressures acting upon a writer: juggling between responsibilities and work; prioritizing health; making and somehow slowing down time; even, perhaps, the arresting, infinite possibilities of the page. Not to mention, all the subconscious terrain, where one wrestles with memory, vulnerability, and presence.

And yet—

These five pieces, selected as the winners by novelist and short story writer Elizabeth McCracken for the 2026 Insider Prize, are awe-inspiring depictions of fortitude, honesty, and the power of narrative—all written under the difficult circumstances found within the carceral system.

Take, for example, Charles Hill’s winning story, “Prisoner’s Home”: where a protagonist returns after serving a lengthy sentence and struggles to adjust to societal conditions. Hill expresses, in earnest, the fears of being seen in public spaces, such as a grocery store, hounded by personal questions—an all-too relatable scenario, regardless of one’s background. (In an interesting turn of events, Charles Hill was discharged sometime after submitting for the prize; his whereabouts are currently unknown. Here’s hoping his personal odyssey leads him to safe harbors.) And Brian Steven’s runner-up story, “A Hairy Tale,” follows a character desperately seeking to rid his cell from his celly’s hair with vivid use of detail and a suspenseful ending.

Deanna Carney’s winning essay, “Sit. Stay.,” recounts heartbreaking events from childhood to parenthood, marked by the various pets that provided comfort in those moments. With prose akin to poetry, she delves into the layers of trauma and finds a way out through healing and support. (A notable event, too: Deanna will be released on parole in late September 2026.) And in a first for the Insider Prize, there are two runners-up in nonfiction, with thought-provoking insights of the system and a portrayal of yearning to reunite with family; Matthew Mendoza’s “Zen and the Art of Civil Commitment” reaches emotional depths through powerful reflections in search of redemption, while Steven Perez’s “Aunt Terry and Josiah King” transports the reader inside his bunker where he makes a call to his dying aunt.

Each submission received for the prize—handwritten or typed out, then mailed in thick, delicate envelopes—examined the human condition through a diverse lens: the lack of justice, oppressive Texas heat in harsh living conditions, violence suffered by transgender women, and the struggle with addiction. Most moving, above all, are the correspondences with the writers themselves who reach out at their own expense—quite literally. A message to touch base and say hello, an eager inquiry on the next open window for the contest, a half-torn, crumbled page from someone asking for writing resources in penciled scribbles. I can only imagine, through slivers of their reality depicted in their pieces, the limited spaces and time allotted; it serves us well to keep in mind the effort and length incarcerated writers undertake for the chance of expression and connection.

With much gratitude from our Insider Prize Assistant Editors, our partners at Lit Hub and Huston-Tillotson University, and everyone at American Short Fiction, I hope these remarkable stories serve as beacons for hope, forgiveness, and redemption. A pause to reflect and a reminder of our privileges, the responsibility to uplift marginalized voices, and the opportunity to meet ourselves on the page—and each other—with the same strength, humility, and grace.

–Sergio Muro, Insider Prize Director

First place, Fiction:
Charles Hill, “Prisoner’s Home”

“Prisoner’s Home,” by Charles Hill, follows a young man in the months after his release from prison, as he discovers that the features of his incarceration—the fights he’s been in, the lies he’s told, the way he’s tried to make himself invulnerable—all follow him home. His given name is Chris, but in prison he calls himself “Crazy.” This complicated and heartfelt story is about how the lies you tell yourself about who you are will change you, but never in the way you hope: what you hope will save you might doom you instead.

–Elizabeth McCracken

Prisoner’s Home
by Charles Hill

Chris went to prison at the young age of nineteen—he was in his second year of college. Photos of Chris on social media show him hunting, drinking, and dancing: all the things his parents never had the opportunity to do.

Prison turned Chris into a liar. After prison, even he couldn’t accept the truth: he had learned to hate freedom and lied about loving home.

***

His American Dream was going well, until one night at a party.

“Hey girl, what’s your name?”

Chris stood up and placed a hand between his girl and the kid who approached her. “Buzz off, buddy. She’s not interested,” Chris said.

The kid stepped back, raising both hands in defense. “Woooow bro, I’m just here to party.” He gave a shitty grin, then glanced at his buddies behind him.

Chris lowered his hand.

“So, girl: are you going to stay with the lame Captain Save-a-Ho or come with big daddy?”

Chris dashed the kid with his drink and swung furiously; he caught him in the jaw with a second swing, the kid dropping like a wet noodle. Two bodyguards turned and walked off. But Chris wasn’t done: he dropped to one knee and pounded the kid’s face. Blow after blow, Chris saw red. He didn’t feel the soft hand or long blond hair rest on the back of his neck or hear the sweet voice crying, “Stop, Chris. Please. Stop.”

Smash, smash, smash.

Someone hit Chris over the head, and the next thing he could remember was a bright white LED shining into his eyes.

“Yep, he’s up now. Drag him to the car,” a cop said.

***

The county jail was a new experience for Chris to say the least, a new one that would last for years. He was charged with aggravated assault; that didn’t stop him from telling everyone he was in for murder. The first thing Chris did was invent a tough sobriquet. Crazy was what he went by now.

Three months later, the DA offered him fifteen years. Everyone on the pod said fifteen was good for murder, so he signed for it.

***

The photos of Crazy that his mom collected were only from visitation. In the first few, Crazy was heavy with weight (which he said gave him more power in his punch) and discolored eyes (which he said was from all the fights he won). This one was a broken nose. This one he had his arm in a cast. The rest are full of deep, deep depression (which he said was from homesick fever).

“Why are all the backgrounds so different?” Susan, Chris’s sister, asked.

“Oh, he has been in so many units: Garza West, Garza East, Beto, Connley, Alred, Coffield, Michaels,” Mom said.

“What for?” Susan asked.

“Heaven knows, Chris’s always said he got into fights but couldn’t talk about them.”

Crazy never told the same story twice. He was all you could be at any given day and had the tattoos to prove it: Crazy’s arms and back were covered with hook tattoos that had thick black lines, pepper shading, and tons of skulls—he even had the state of Texas on his neck.

***

The last two weeks before Crazy was released on parole, he gathered all the personal information of fellow inmates he could. With a smile and a hug, he told them he would keep in touch. Crazy even told all his close friends he was going to send them money to buy snacks. But the last two days, his pretentious promises ate at his insides; he hovered over the toilet all night puking the pork noodle casserole. He puked so much, it seemed like he had puked all the casserole trays he had ever eaten in the past decade—which is a lot of pork noodle. The truth was he wasn’t ready to leave. He had never prepared to leave. But Crazy was never going to tell that.

Crazy wore ‘70s throwback Salvation Army clothes and stood at the last gate between him and freedom, the closest he had been in ten years. The air was fresher, the sky was baby blue and deep with no clouds. The trees played music with the wind as it sifted through their branches.

He exhaled. “Okay, okay, okay,” he whispered, squeezing his hand and looking down at the scars over his knuckle.

“Gate!” an officer behind him yelled.

Crazy’s body shrunk hearing the voice. Did I do something wrong? Are they going to let me go?

Click. The door popped open, and the gate swung out with a creak.

“Go on boy. Ain’t gonna shoot you. You’re free,” the office said, giving him a shove.

Crazy’s right leg stepped on the uneven concrete; for a moment, he felt like Armstrong. One small step for man. His mind reeled like a movie: steps, hugs and kisses from Mom and sis. Breathe. Sit in the car. Breathe. Soft seat, gone. Breathe, gone. Out of sight. Breathe.

The piny woods swallowed the red bricks surrounded by spirals of razor wire and fence. He felt like his heart was plucked from his chest.

***

“Oh, Chris, wait until we get you something to eat,” Mom squawked. His dad said nothing. Susan said nothing. Crazy said nothing.

“Chris, quit looking back,” Mom said with a sap smile.

“Huh? Oh, okay.” Breathe, Crazy thought.

The first five years in prison, all Crazy wanted was a homecoming party, but the last five years, he didn’t want anything.

“Well, here we are. We’re home! Come on, Chris. No one’s here. Just you, Susan, me, and Dad,” Mom said.

Crazy sat on the swing under the oak tree: no party, no friends, just family. The only people who reached out to him the entire ten years. Nothing was the same. The house was painted brown. All the bikes were rusted, and everyone’s vehicles were new. But it was just like he liked it, he told himself. He sat on the swing until the sun went down, alone, just like he wanted.

Dinner decked the table: golden buttery mashed potatoes, roast beef with draining juices seeping out the sides, greens with chunks of soggy bacon gasping for air.

“Just like you always liked it, after a big Friday night game,” Mom said.

“Just like I liked it. Thanks, Mom.” Crazy slapped a heap of potatoes on his plate.

Dad forked a bite of roast beef, eyed it, then shoved it in his mouth.

His sister stared at Crazy with amazement. “Chris, now that there’s no one listening to the phone calls, tell us some real stories.” Susan’s eyes beamed.

The potatoes on Crazy’s spoon, once golden butter, turned to prison-styled potatoes: rotten with black spots and brown potato skins. He dropped the spoon, stopped chewing.

The clock on the wall clicked its small, plastic hands. A small, black radio in the living room, just over a whisper, played a George Strait song.

“The real story . . . you see, well I . . .” Crazy stopped to wipe the water in his eyes.

“Oh Chris, it’s okay. Tell us another time, honey,” Mom said.

“Yeah. Susan, you can’t ask big questions like that. That answer’s going to take weeks to tell,” Crazy said.

“Okay, do you have a good fight story?” Susan probed.

“Which one?” Crazy wiped his forehead, then trailed his finger over the scar above his eyebrow.

“You got more than one?” She leaned over her plate.

“What, do you think it’s a walk down a church pew? Everyone’s a criminal.”

Dinner floated by with vapid comments around the meal and eventually died out.

***

After dinner, Crazy laid down in his own bed and was transported to another time: one he no longer recognized—the time every minute was precious. The bed felt soft, softer than it had ever felt. Time ticked up to twelve, then started down. In the dark, Crazy couldn’t tell if his eyes were open or closed. His mind ran the perimeter of the room, visualizing the window, door, walls, and photos. Silence rang in his ears, listening to himself breathe. Blood streamed through his veins, pulsing inside him, like a ticking time bomb. The bed turned stiff and hard; he felt uncomfortable, alienated.

A dream haunted him: Somebody, somewhere, chasing him. Room after room, he slammed the doors behind him for safety, but the doors were never the right size to fit the frame; they were smaller, half the size. Run, run, run. Twisting in blank abandoned rooms like a maze with no end, but no time to stop. No time to rest.

“Chris!”

“Huh? Yeah?” Crazy said.

“Get up. Coffee’s ready,” Dad said.

“Yeah.” Crazy ran his hands over his face, trying to relax. “I’ll be out in a minute.” He rolled out of bed and shuffled to the porch.

“Black?” Dad asked, rocking back on a wooden chair.

“Yeah, that’s all I drink anymore.”

“That’s good,” he said, handing Crazy the other cup on the coffee table. “It’ll put hair on your chest.” Dad smiled and slurped the top of his cup.

“When I worked in the fields, I used to watch the sun come up like this,” Crazy said.

“Fields?”

“Hoe squad. Fields. It’s the worst job. The same job as slaves in America: picking vegetables and cutting grass with a hoe,” Crazy said.

“Sounds like a good job for youngsters trying to knock the edge off.”

“You would think, but that’s where I got into my first fight.”

“Ahh? You win?” Dad leaned in, staring at Crazy.

“Yeah, well almost. But winning’s not always a win because both of you lose—and a loss is a win. So, a fight is a win-win or a loss. Out of the hundred and five fights I’ve had, I’ve never lost one.”

“Son, I don’t think you woke up yet.” Dad glanced down at Crazy’s cup.

Crazy looked out at the sheen of the dew covering the grass. “The grass is what started it,” Crazy said in a daze. “The lead row said I wasn’t cleaning my row.” Crazy trailed off, searching the vast blue sky. “Then, he called me a white boy. That was when Krooked Kracker elbowed me and threw a shoulder up.” Crazy swallowed. “That’s when I knew I had to. So, I yelled back, ‘You’re a boy, boy.’ They all stopped rocking after that. Well, the black ones. They threw down their aggies.” Crazy sat the cup on the table. “I got two swings in. He got me in the eye. I hit the dirt and got pepper sprayed. Then, the lieutenant fired his pistol.” Crazy tapped his fingers on his leg. “I never missed a blade of grass after that or wasn’t called out on it.” Crazy picked up the cold coffee and swallowed a big gulp. “I never missed a blade of grass. Never.”

Dad sat his cup down, stood up to leave, then said, “It was better the last time you told me that story.”

Crazy watched Dad’s car head to work until it faded into the horizon. His phone buzzed. His thumbs fumbled with the touchscreen. “Damn screen, where’s the buttons at?” Twenty minutes later, he texted Nathan back: Yeah, come over, bro. I’m at the house chillin.

***

When Nathan arrived, he walked up the porch and gave Crazy a big homecoming hug. Crazy couldn’t keep his eyes from watering; he wasn’t sure if it was the hug or compassion. They sat on the porch with a round of fresh coffee.

“Yeah, prison is like a fight club: the more time you do, the better you get,” Crazy said.

“So, you ever get your ass whooped?” Nathan asked.

“Hell no. I never lost a fight.” Crazy’s hand shook, sipping the lies down with black gold.

“I remember this one time, I sold a watch and the guy said, ‘Oh, you’re jacked.’ That’s when I stole off on him,” Crazy said.

“Stole off?”

“I hit him in the mouth, took his tooth out with that punch. Took my watch and the black bag he had.”

“Black bag?”

“Instant coffee. It’s trash, really. After that, they shipped me. The law said I was a danger.” Crazy pulled air through his teeth. “How many fights have you been in out here?”

“Uhh,” Nathan blushed. “None. No one fights out here.”

“Oh,” Crazy relaxed. “No one fights?”

“If you fight at work, you’re fired.”

“No fights? What happens if someone disrespects you? You know, calls you out of your name?”

“Uhh, you, well, they don’t.” Nathan cast his eyes down to his phone. “Well, I’ve got to go, Chris. Got to pick the kids up.”

“Oh yeah. Don’t you have a son?”

“I got three. They all popped out a year apart. The oldest is in third grade.”

Crazy looked at Nathan’s young face, wondering if he looked like a father.

***

The next three months, Crazy stayed in his room. He was stuck on TikTok and YouTube, looking up prison stories: gangs, fights, horrors, and testimonies. Prison, prison, prison. He learned more about prison than a prisoner knew. He learned so much, he felt it built up on him, pushing him to a new standard: super penitentiary.

“Super penitentiary, yeah,” Crazy said out loud.

Crazy was confined to his room. He didn’t like the feeling of opening doors; when he did, he closed them quickly. The only time he left the house was on foot to visit the local HEB. He pushed an empty cart. He loved to admire the flashy, plastic logos, different varieties of chips, and junk food. As soon as he passed another shopper, he stiffened and furled his eyebrows. Crazy looked into shoppers’ eyes like he was going to say: What? Say something.

But he was scared—scared of the questions they would ask about his tattoos. He knew they knew. He felt everyone knew he was fresh out.

Crazy hated seeing fellow convicts. He could spot them easily: the way they walked and the black ink on their body. He always quickened his pace and gave a strong nod. His body turned into a robotic character on a mission to some important place—which was never the case for Crazy—but he felt the need to lie with his body. The most terrifying conversation Crazy could think of was the one where he was working, how he was adjusting, because truthfully, he was tired of lying.

***

One day, Crazy sat at the dinner table eating a bowl of Top Ramen noodle soup.

“Chris, you know it’s May?” Mom said.

“May?” Chris slurped noodles.

“The summer is coming. You know how much work goes on in the summer?”

“Yeah, and it’s hot.”

“Chris, it’s been six months. It’s been long enough. Your father told me to tell you to take his truck out.”

“Drive his truck?! The Silverado? That thing is big.”

“Don’t start with me! It’s the same size as your old truck,” Mom said.

“I never had a truck. I’ve never had a job.” Crazy picked the bowl up and chugged down the salty, yellow sludge. “They want to see past work history. I ain’t got any.”

“Chris, honey. You can’t get history if you don’t get a job.”

“The jobs are history. Didn’t you see what the news said about AI?! It’s going to take all our jobs!”

Mom grabbed the rag on the table and wiped the clean corner, dumped the rag in the sink, then turned to Crazy. “The keys are on the hook.”

Crazy grabbed the keys, got in the truck, and headed down the road. The pressure of doing something for the first time compounded. Every lie Crazy told about the job he had in the past rattled in his head, like bouncing marbles. Crazy was so used to doing nothing; the thought of doing anything triggered his fight or flight. Job, car, housing, insurance, bills, wife, kids: all equaled responsibility. Life was too complicated for Crazy. He couldn’t lie himself out of this one, so he did the only thing he knew would bring him home.

***

Main Street was as dead as it had always been, but the courthouse was busy as a beehive swarming with squad cars. Crazy locked eyes on a trooper as he rolled through the four way. The light turned green. Crazy froze. His heart leaped inside his chest.

The cop stared at him and the front license plate. Crazy stomped on the gas, burning the back tires.

Lights flickered, red and blue. The chase only took ten minutes.

Crazy jumped out before parking the truck and laid down on the soft asphalt. He grinned when the cold handcuffs clicked around his wrists. He laughed when the cop screamed at him to answer the questions. Crazy relaxed when he sat on the hard plastic backseat; he felt free looking through the metal bars lining the windows. The plexiglass in front of him had scratches that appeared random until he looked closer. He could make out the words: super penitentiary.

“Well, Superman, you’re headed back to the pen,” the cop said.

***

Crazy sat on a rusted, circular stool in a cold hard cell. He flipped open a copy of The Odyssey. The question dawned on him: Could a warrior ever return home?

Runner-up, Fiction:
Brian Stevens, “A Hairy Tale”

“The hair was another animal entirely.” Funny, dark, surreal, and completely surprising: “A Hairy Tale” by Brian Stevens follows the weird life of the narrator’s cellmate’s hair. It is also deeply strange, in the best possible way.

–Elizabeth McCracken

A Hairy Tale
by Brian Stevens

My celly’s hair is a nightmare. The stuff just goes everywhere. Every morning, my first chore is to wipe all his hair off the floor. I clean the cell to no avail.

***

Ants occupied the cell when I first arrived. They crawled in through the cracks and marched along the walls. Any food or flesh that crossed their paths was quickly devoured. Their bites would leave itchy red welts on my hands and feet. I fought them tooth and nail with everything I had: baby powder, soap, shampoo, laundry detergent, bleach. I was able to slow them down; as summer ended, the weather cooled and they eventually went away. Then, only the hair remained.

***

The hair was another animal together, but unlike the ants, it could not be contained. The fans in the cell created tornadoes of tangles that clung to anything they touched. There was hair on my bed; my clothes; in my mouth and nose; my coffee when I took a drink; and the drain when I used the sink. Hair came back around, got stuck in the fans, and when I rinsed my washcloth, hair stuck to my hands. The hair began to take on a life of its own: no matter how much I cleaned, I was never alone.

The hairs were long, black, and curly like the pubes of a buffalo. Bundles of them would roll across the ground like tumbleweeds blowing in the wind of the Wild West. Sometimes, I would mistake a stray strand for a cockroach as it scurried from one side of the cell to the other. Hairs strung along the shelves like broken spiderwebs in abandoned basements. The black hairs were bad, but the white ones were worse: they were invisible to the naked eye and could hide in plain sight. They were ghosts of dead hairs past that would continue to haunt me for eternity. Something drastic had to be done.

***

No ordinary razor would ever be able to chop down that forest of frizz. I searched for some scissors but had to settle for a shank—a dirty guy named Sanchez sold it to me for six soups and seven shots of coffee. He told me it was so sharp, it could slit a pig’s throat with a single slice. I took his word and kept it carefully wrapped in a johnny sack. I certainly did not want to get caught with such a serious piece of contraband, so I had to act soon.

That night, I asked my celly to cut his hair; he refused. He knew it made a mess everyday but didn’t seem very concerned about cleaning it up. He was also deeply religious and claimed his hair gave him strength like Samson.

As he drank himself to sleep, I thought about cutting some of his hair but then decided it all needed to be shaved. Upon further inspection, I realized: even with a shaved head, his hair would still grow back, and that would never do. No, his whole head would have to come off.
